content.text:
Assuming you mean **the first artificial satellite vs. modern/latest satellites**:

| Feature | **First satellite: Sputnik 1** | **Latest modern satellites** |
|---|---|---|
| **Launch date** | October 4, 1957 | Satellites launch almost weekly; examples in 2026 include Starlink, Earth-observation, military, and broadband constellations |
| **Country/organization** | Soviet Union | Many: SpaceX, NASA, ESA, China, India, Amazon, military agencies, universities, private firms |
| **Size/mass** | 58 cm sphere; 83.6 kg | Ranges from tiny CubeSats under 10 kg to multi-ton communications satellites |
| **Main purpose** | Prove an object could orbit Earth; transmit simple radio beeps | Internet, GPS/navigation, weather, climate monitoring, military surveillance, science, disaster response, phone connectivity |
| **Technology** | Basic radio transmitter, batteries, antennas | Solar panels, onboard computers, AI/autonomous systems, high-speed radios, cameras, radar, electric propulsion |
| **Lifetime** | Batteries lasted about 21 days; re-entered in January 1958 | Months to 15+ years depending on mission |
| **Communication** | Simple “beep” radio signal | Broadband internet, laser links, encrypted military data, real-time Earth imagery |
| **Orbit** | Low Earth orbit; about 98 minutes per orbit | Low, medium, geostationary, lunar, interplanetary orbits |
| **Cost/access** | Government superpower project | Much cheaper and more routine; private companies launch thousands of satellites |

**In short:** Sputnik 1 was basically a metal ball with a radio transmitter that proved spaceflight was possible. Modern satellites are highly capable computers in space that can deliver internet, map Earth in detail, guide GPS, monitor weather, and support global communications.

NASA describes Sputnik 1 as the world’s first artificial satellite, about beach-ball sized, weighing 83.6 kg, and orbiting Earth every ~98 minutes. ([nasa.gov](https://www.nasa.gov/history/dawn-of-the-space-age/?utm_source=openai)) As of 2026, satellite launches are routine; for example, Arianespace announced a June 17, 2026 mission to launch 36 Amazon Leo broadband satellites into low Earth orbit. ([newsroom.arianespace.com](https://newsroom.arianespace.com/arianespace-to-launch-36-amazon-leo-satellites-with-an-ariane-64-equipped-with-advanced-boosters-on-june-17-2026/?lang=eng&utm_source=openai))
